title: India's battery storage self-sufficiency remains over a decade away
gist: Wood Mackenzie finds India's domestic battery cell manufacturing (2 GWh commissioned versus China's 2,695 GWh) covers under 1% of 2026 tender demand, and despite a globally competitive underlying cost base, execution delays, financing gaps and deep dependence on Chinese and Korean technology licensors mean true cell self-sufficiency is 10-15 years away - the nearer-term opportunity is downstream component localisation.

insights.claim: India's domestic battery cell manufacturing covers less than 1% of the country's roughly 260 GWh demand pipeline from 2026 competitive tenders, leaving the market structurally reliant on imports even as policy ambition accelerates.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Import dependence for battery storage hardware will persist for years - track import volumes and forex/supply-chain exposure for Indian BESS developers.
insights.quote: India's domestic battery manufacturing currently accounts for less than 1% of its approximately 260 GWh demand pipeline from competitive tenders in 2026

insights.claim: Despite more than 226 GWh of battery cell manufacturing capacity announced for construction through 2035, India remains 10 to 15 years away from a globally competitive, self-sufficient cell industry because of execution delays, financing viability challenges and deep technology dependence on Chinese and Korean licensors.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Don't price in near-term Indian battery cell self-sufficiency; the addressable domestic supply-chain opportunity is a decade-plus theme, not a near-term one.
insights.quote: India remains 10 to 15 years from a globally competitive, self-sufficient cell industry.

themes.theme: China's supply-chain dominance as the benchmark

insights.claim: India has only 2 GWh of commissioned battery cell manufacturing capacity as of 2026, versus China's cumulative capacity of 2,695 GWh - a scale gap of roughly three orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The absolute scale gap versus China is the clearest evidence that India's self-sufficiency timeline is measured in decades, not years.
insights.quote: India has just 2 GWh of commissioned cell manufacturing capacity as of 2026, against China's cumulative capacity of 2,695 GWh.

insights.claim: China controls between 85% and 98% of global battery supply-chain capacity across every major component - cathode, anode, separator and electrolyte - meaning any country's localisation push must displace a near-monopolistic incumbent across the whole chain, not just at cell assembly.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: China's dominance is upstream-materials-wide, not just cell assembly - any diversification thesis has to account for cathode/anode/separator/electrolyte capacity, not only gigafactories.
insights.quote: China controls between 85% and 98% of global capacity across every major supply chain component, from cathode to anode, separator and electrolyte.

insights.claim: India is prioritising localisation of downstream components - containers, energy management systems, SCADA and battery packs - over the next two to three years, backed by a new 20% domestic content requirement (DCR) applied to grid-scale BESS projects under new tenders.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Component-level localisation (packs, EMS, containers) is the nearer-term investable opportunity in Indian BESS versus cell manufacturing.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie modelling shows that scaling India's domestic content requirement from under 20% to 100% would add about a 30% total capex premium to a benchmark 100 MW, two-hour battery storage project.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A move toward 100% DCR would materially raise the cost of Indian grid-scale storage - a key input for tender pricing and project IRR modelling.
insights.quote: scaling domestic content requirements (DCR) from less than 20% to 100% adds about 30% total CAPEX premium to a benchmark 100 MW, 2-hour battery storage project

themes.theme: Cost economics: premium at home, advantage abroad

insights.claim: Locally manufactured battery cells in India are expected to cost 25-40% more than imported cells, driven by limited manufacturing scale, higher financing costs and an underdeveloped supplier ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Buyers will keep favoring imported cells on cost until scale and supplier depth improve, even as DCR rules push localisation.
insights.quote: locally manufactured cells are expected to cost 25-40% more than imported ones
insights.locator: A competitive cost position, but a premium over China

insights.claim: India's underlying manufacturing cost base is globally competitive, offering a 154% cost advantage over Japan and a 9% advantage over South Korea - ranking second only to China among major battery manufacturing destinations.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: India's structural cost position could still attract supply-chain diversification capital away from China despite the near-term import cost gap.
insights.quote: India's underlying cost position is globally competitive by offering a 154% cost advantage over Japan and a 9% advantage over South Korea, placing it second only to China among major manufacturing destinations.
insights.locator: A competitive cost position, but a premium over China

insights.claim: Indian cell manufacturing is expected to rely on imported inputs for the next two to five years, while building full domestic refining capabilities will take more than ten years.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Refining self-sufficiency, not cell assembly, is the longer pole in the tent for true Indian battery independence.
insights.locator: A competitive cost position, but a premium over China

insights.claim: Only four players have commissioned gigafactories in India as of 2026, with financial viability remaining a central obstacle to scaling further.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A very small, concentrated set of operators currently defines India's battery manufacturing base - watch these four for execution signals.
insights.quote: Only four players have commissioned gigafactories in India as of 2026

insights.claim: A 5 GWh battery cell facility in India operates at roughly -10% EBITDA; breakeven is only achievable near 10 GWh of scale, and positive margins require at least 20 GWh - implying most currently planned Indian gigafactories are sub-scale and financially unviable without further consolidation or capital.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Scale is the binary determinant of gigafactory viability in India - screen announced projects against the roughly 20 GWh profitability threshold before assuming they will reach positive margins.
insights.quote: a 5 GWh facility operates at -10% EBITDA, with breakeven only achievable at 10 GWh and positive margins requiring at least 20 GWh

insights.claim: Nearly all Indian battery cell players depend on Chinese or Korean technology licences, which limits their control over pricing and supply chains and keeps them technologically subordinate to their licensors.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Licensing dependence caps the pricing power and margin upside of Indian battery manufacturers even as installed capacity scales up.
insights.quote: Nearly all players rely on Chinese or Korean technology licences, which limit their control over pricing and supply chains.

themes.theme: Analyst framing: policy intent vs. execution

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's director for the report frames India's battery ambitions as credible in intent but constrained by a wide gap between policy and operational capacity, arguing the near-term opportunity lies in downstream components rather than cells, and that closing the cell-industry gap will require sustained investment well beyond current incentive schemes.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frame Indian battery-storage investment across two horizons: a near-term downstream/component localisation play and a decade-plus cell self-sufficiency thesis that current incentive schemes alone won't fund.
insights.quote: India's battery storage ambitions are credible, but the gap between policy intent and operational capacity is wide
insights.locator: quote attributed to Ankita Chauhan, director, Wood Mackenzie

insights.claim: A Wood Mackenzie senior analyst frames India's competitive cost position as a genuine strategic asset for global supply-chain diversification, contingent on closing the execution gap before other emerging manufacturing hubs capture the same opportunity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch whether India can execute fast enough to capture supply-chain diversification capital before competing emerging hubs do - a time-sensitive window rather than a guaranteed win.
insights.quote: India's cost position is genuinely competitive in a global context, and that matters as supply chain diversification becomes a strategic imperative
insights.locator: quote attributed to Priya Shrivastava, Senior Research Analyst, Wood Mackenzie
